entries.name: Delayed-rejection Metropolis
entries.definition: A Metropolis-Hastings sampling procedure that can propose another candidate after rejection within the same transition, correcting acceptance for the probabilities of the forward and reversed rejected paths.
entries.identity_notes: This is the path-reversal delayed-rejection construction in Mira Sections 2–3. Rejected internal candidates are auxiliary information; the chain remains at its original state until a candidate is accepted or the transition ends. It differs from across-iteration adaptive Metropolis and from independent repeated accept-reject generation. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: For current x with pi(x)>0, propose y1 from q1(x,·) and use a1(x,y1)=min(1,pi(y1)q1(y1,x)/(pi(x)q1(x,y1))). If rejected, draw y2 from q2(x,y1,·). Accept y2 with min(1, [pi(y2)q1(y2,y1)q2(y2,y1,x)(1−a1(y2,y1))]/[pi(x)q1(x,y1)q2(x,y1,y2)(1−a1(x,y1))]). The zero reverse-path case has acceptance zero. A fixed two-stage implementation retains x if both tests reject. Higher stages require the corresponding reversed-path proposal and previous-rejection products; simply applying ordinary Metropolis to each retry omits those factors.
entries.locator: Section 2, Equations (1)–(4), printed pp. 232–234 / PDF pp. 2–4; Section 4, pp. 238–240 / PDF pp. 8–10
limitations: Proposal support and well-defined forward-path probabilities are required; formulas apply to reachable rejection paths. Irreducibility and convergence need further conditions beyond detailed balance.
The record gives the explicit two-stage rule and identifies the higher-stage construction, not a claim that every history-dependent retry is valid.
Extra stages cost proposal and target evaluations. Per-transition asymptotic-variance comparisons do not guarantee faster estimates per unit computation.
A finite stage cap retains the original state after all rejections. Eventual acceptance is not guaranteed for unrestricted retry schemes.

entries.name: Symmetric delayed rejection
entries.definition: The delayed-rejection specialization using the same symmetric proposal kernel at every stage, centered through the last rejected candidate, with acceptance determined by the largest previous rejected target density.
entries.identity_notes: This record is the fixed-kernel specialization in Mira Section 3. The next proposal depends on the last rejected point rather than being recentered on the unchanged chain state. Stage-dependent variances and generic symmetric proposals do not automatically satisfy the cancellations used by this simplified rule. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: Let q(a,b)=q(b,a) be the same kernel at every stage. Starting from x, propose y1 from q(x,·) and accept with min(1,pi(y1)/pi(x)). After i−1 rejections, propose yi from q(y(i−1),·), set M=max_{j<i} pi(yj), and accept with min(1,max(0,(pi(yi)−M)/(pi(x)−M))). On a reachable rejection path, M<pi(x). If a chosen finite stage limit is exhausted, retain x. Accepted candidates end the transition; rejected candidates do not become chain states. The formula follows cancellation of the forward and reverse path terms under the fixed symmetric-kernel assumption.
entries.locator: Section 3, displayed fixed-kernel assumption and Equations (6)–(9), printed pp. 234–236 / PDF pp. 4–6; Figure 1 and continuation discussion, pp. 237–238 / PDF pp. 7–8
limitations: Figure 1 prints pi(x)/pi(y1) for its first-stage nontrivial acceptance region, reversing the correct pi(y1)/pi(x) in the preceding text. This record uses the text and general Metropolis formula; the figure discrepancy was visually inspected.

The later suggestion to decrease variance by stage is not treated as permission to use this simplified acceptance with arbitrary changing q. Such proposals need the general delayed-rejection correction.

A candidate whose target density is no larger than the maximum target density among previous rejected candidates is rejected. No finite-time eventual-acceptance or universal efficiency guarantee is asserted.
Detailed balance is not a substitute for support, irreducibility and numerical-stability checks.

entries.name: Multiple-try Metropolis
entries.definition: A Metropolis sampling algorithm that selects a candidate from several weighted forward proposals, draws a backward reference set containing the original state, and corrects acceptance using the ratio of their total weights.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers Liu–Liang–Wong Section 2 finite-k MTM with one proposal kernel and a symmetric weight factor. It is not simple selection of the highest-density candidate, importance resampling without a correction, or the general auxiliary-variable extension in Section 3.1. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: Choose k≥1, a proposal T with T(a,b)>0 iff T(b,a)>0, and nonnegative symmetric lambda positive wherever T is positive. Define w(a,b)=pi(a)T(a,b)lambda(a,b). From current x, draw k independent yj from T(x,·), and select y with probabilities proportional to w(yj,x). Draw k−1 independent xj* from T(y,·), and append xk*=x. Accept y with min(1,sum_j w(yj,x)/sum_j w(xj*,y)); otherwise retain x. For k=1 the symmetric lambda cancels, recovering Metropolis-Hastings. Selection and the backward reference set are essential to this correction.
entries.locator: Section 2, Equations (2)–(5), numbered algorithm and Theorem 1, printed p. 122 / PDF p. 2; Section 7 discussion, p. 133 / PDF p. 13; Section 3.1 weight-order discrepancy, p. 123 / PDF p. 3
limitations: Weight sums must be finite and usable. If all forward candidates have zero target weight, the transition can be completed by retaining x; weighted selection is not performed with a zero denominator.
The number of proposals and target evaluations grows with k. Larger k does not imply universal improvement per unit computation or independent retained draws.

The auxiliary-variable extension in Section 3.1 prints selection weights with an argument order inconsistent with Section 2 and its own acceptance expression. That extension is not asserted by this record.
Target invariance under the stated construction does not alone establish irreducibility or a mixing rate.

entries.name: Multiple-try Metropolis within Gibbs
entries.definition: A coordinate-update sampler that applies a multiple-try Metropolis transition to a conditional target while holding all other coordinates fixed.
entries.identity_notes: This is the MTM-Gibbs construction in Liu–Liang–Wong Section 5.2, a specific multiple-candidate Metropolis-within-Gibbs kernel. It need not draw exactly from a full conditional in one update and does not replace that conditional with a gridded interpolation. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: For a chosen coordinate i, fix x_−i and use the unnormalized scalar target pi_i(z)=pi(x_−i,z). Draw k independent yj from T(x_i,·), compute w(yj,x_i)=pi_i(yj)T(yj,x_i)lambda(yj,x_i), and select y in proportion to these weights. Draw k−1 reference values from T(y,·), append the old x_i, and accept using the forward-to-reference total-weight ratio of MTM. On acceptance replace only coordinate i; otherwise keep the full state. T may depend on the fixed remaining coordinates; its forward/reverse support and symmetric lambda requirements hold within that conditional update.
entries.locator: Section 5.2, MTM-Gibbs steps 1–3, printed p. 126 / PDF p. 6, with Section 2 Equation (3), p. 122 / PDF p. 2
limitations: This is conditional target invariance, not an exact independent conditional draw or independence of successive full states.
Use the complete backward-reference correction. Keeping only the weighted candidate selection defines a different procedure.
Zero forward total weight is handled by retaining the current coordinate; finite, meaningful target/proposal weights are required.
Support, coordinate scheduling and irreducibility determine whether the full chain can explore the target. No benchmark advantage over Gibbs or other conditional kernels is asserted.

entries.name: Conjugate-gradient Monte Carlo
entries.definition: A population Markov sampler that obtains a local-optimization anchor from one population member and updates another member along the anchor line with a multiple-try transition targeting a radial-Jacobian-adjusted density.
entries.identity_notes: This is Liu–Liang–Wong Section 4.2 CGMC, not the conjugate-gradient linear solver or direct optimization as a substitute for sampling. Its anchor comes from a different stream. The product target is an invariant population law, not a statement that transient streams are independent. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: Maintain m≥2 population members targeting a product of pi. Choose a reference member x_r uniformly at random, and deterministically optimize along a gradient or conjugate-gradient direction of log pi to obtain anchor A=g(x_r). Choose x_c uniformly among the other members. For A≠x_c, define e=(A−x_c)/||A−x_c|| and the scalar line target f(r) proportional to |r|^(d−1)pi(A+r e), r on the whole real line. Apply a valid MTM transition along this line, starting at the scalar coordinate of x_c, and replace x_c by A+r_new e while retaining the other members. A scalar proposal and weight construction must respect the same unoriented line when traversed in reverse; a centered Gaussian scalar random-walk proposal of fixed variance with MTM-II target-density selection weights is a concrete compatible choice. The source’s product-invariance argument uses the anchor’s independence from the moved member under the product target.
entries.locator: Sections 4.1–4.2, CGMC steps 1–3, Equation (11), Theorem 2 and Lemma 1, printed pp. 124–125 / PDF pp. 4–5; population diagnostic caveat and discussion, p. 133 / PDF p. 13; Section 2 MTM-II choice, p. 122 / PDF p. 2
limitations: The factor |r|^(d−1) is essential for an anchor line selected through the current point. Replacing the line target with pi(A+r e) alone is not this construction.
The optimization anchor must be independent of the moved member under the product stationary law. Optimizing that same member and copying this acceptance scheme is not justified.

The zero-length line A=x_c requires a defined degenerate-case policy; the displayed normalized direction is not evaluated at zero. Differentiability and the chosen deterministic optimization procedure have their own requirements.
The compatible scalar-proposal statement is an explicit implementation constraint inferred from reversing the unoriented line, not a new algorithm attributed to the source.
Invariance does not guarantee population exploration, convergence, independent transient streams or universally reliable convergence diagnostics. Optimization and multiple trials add cost.

entries.name: Robust adaptive Metropolis
entries.definition: An adaptive random-walk Metropolis algorithm that updates the proposal shape factor by a rank-one transformation driven by the proposal direction and the difference between its acceptance probability and a chosen target rate.
entries.identity_notes: This is Vihola’s RAM update, which avoids estimating the target covariance. It differs from covariance-based adaptive Metropolis, scale-only adaptation and a fixed random-walk kernel. RAM here denotes this sampler, not computer memory. The history-dependent state sequence is not assumed to be a homogeneous Markov chain. No normalized match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 175 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktrees; the only text hit was an unrelated installed-package checksum substring. Existing general Metropolis-Hastings, Metropolis-within-Gibbs and random-walk records were inspected to resolve these specialization boundaries.
entries.mechanism: Let q be a spherical density, S a lower-triangular factor with positive diagonal, x satisfy pi(x)>0, eta_n lie in (0,1] and decay to zero, and alpha_star lie in (0,1). Draw U from q and propose y=x+S U. Set alpha=min(1,pi(y)/pi(x)), accept y with this probability or retain x. Whether accepted or rejected, choose the next positive-diagonal Cholesky factor S_new satisfying S_new S_new^T=S[I+eta_n(alpha−alpha_star)UU^T/||U||²]S^T. The update uses the acceptance probability, not the binary acceptance outcome; the normalized direction U determines the rank-one adjustment. It expands that component when alpha exceeds the target and contracts it when alpha is smaller.
entries.locator: Section 2, steps R1–R3 and Equation (1), Proposition 1 and Remarks 2–4, PDF pp. 3–5; Section 4, Assumptions 12–16, Theorem 17 and Remark 19, pp. 11–13; Section 6, pp. 16–17
limitations: Spherical continuous proposals make U=0 a null event; numerical implementations still need a zero-norm guard and stable factor updates.

Positive definiteness of each update does not prove long-run stability. The source’s strong-law result assumes target/proposal regularity and step-size conditions and holds on an event where shape eigenvalues stay bounded away from zero and infinity.
The paper explicitly leaves unrestricted stability unproved. Enforcing fixed eigenvalue bounds by rejecting a proposed shape update is a separate safeguard that can alter the limiting shape.

A chosen acceptance rate is a tuning target, not a universal optimum or convergence diagnostic. Strong multimodality can remain difficult; no benchmark or arbitrary-heavy-tail convergence guarantee is asserted.
The exact inspected arXiv v2 bytes have a later title-page footer date. This record does not claim to have inspected the later journal version.

source_analysis.interpretation: Read all extracted text. The explicit two-stage correction includes rejected-path probabilities. Fixed symmetric q through the last rejected point gives the maximum-density formula. Figure 1 first-stage ratio is visibly reversed relative to the text; records use the text and general MH rule. The suggested changing stage variance does not automatically retain the fixed-q cancellation. Per-step variance comparisons are not CPU-time guarantees.

The scan required OCR; key definitions, weights, backward set, conditional-coordinate rule, radial Jacobian and product-invariance argument were visually inspected. Section 3.1 weight order differs from core Section 2 and its acceptance expression, so auxiliary MTM and random-ray variants remain deferred. CGMC chooses a distinct reference and moved stream; line-reversal compatibility is an explicitly identified implementation inference. The source warns against treating transient population streams as independent for convergence diagnostics. Numerical experiment pages 7–12 remain unread.

R1–R3 uses acceptance probability and normalized proposal direction, including after rejected moves. Conditional strong-law theorem and explicit stability caveat were read and visually checked. Spherical proposal and Cholesky positivity are not sufficient for general adaptive ergodicity. The footer says 2018 despite version submission in 2011. No benchmark values, unrestricted heavy-tail convergence claim or later journal inspection is asserted.
